newsitem.title: USA: Striking Teamsters cheer tentative deal with UPS.
newsitem.headline: Striking Teamsters cheer tentative deal with UPS.

text.p: Thousands of striking Teamsters cheered a tentative agreement on Tuesday with United Parcel Service that promised to send them back to work with higher pay, more full-time jobs and heftier pension benefits.

For the first time since they began walking picket lines in the stifling summer heat 15 days ago, strikers threw aside union plackards for a jubilant round of hugs, back-slaps and relieved smiles as news of their apparent victory spread.
"This is going to set the tone for a lot of other unions," said Robert Bolden, a UPS delivery van driver in Atlanta who has spent 10 years on part-time status.
"The important thing for me was always that the Teamsters stood strong -- we're a brotherhood," he said.

When news of the tentative agreement reached picket lines across the country late on Monday, Teamster members huddled quietly around radios and television sets in hopes of learning details of the settlement.

Some struggled visibly to contain their emotions as early coverage of the deal focused on pay and pensions but failed to include the issue of full-time jobs, an all-important element of the strike for many who work 40 hours a week or more but remain on part-time status.
"We should have stayed out longer to get everything we need," one striker gloomily remarked.
But soon, news that the agreement included the creation of 10,000 full-time jobs from the existing pool of part-time workers began to circulate among the Teamster rank-and-file.
"This may be your last chance to get on TV," cried one elated picketer as TV news crews rushed up to strikers outside an idle UPS hub facility in the predawn hours, with camera lights glaring.
Part-time workers make up about 60 percent of the 301,000- member UPS work force in the United States, and nearly two- thirds of the company's 185,000 Teamster members.

The agreement, as described by Teamster President Ron Carey at a Washington press conference, would raise part-time wages from $11 to $15 an hour over five years and markedly improve pension benefits under a plan that would remain in union hands.

Until the latest round of marathon talks began five days ago, management had insisted that union pensions be withdrawn from the Teamster plan and re-established under a fund designed solely for UPS employees.
The agreement came three days after Teamster members began receiving their first disbursement of a meager $55 per week in strike benefits.

The strike forced many into a financial juggling act at home. The lack of a weekly paycheck sent some strikers out to look for temporary work, while others scrambled to reach contingent agreements on payments for car loans, rent and mortgages.
The company also threatened more than 15,000 Teamster layoffs to compensate for business lost to the strike.

On Tuesday, strikers lauded the administration of President Bill Clinton for its part in resisting management calls to order the union back to work. The White House instead pressed both sides to continue talking under the auspices of a federal mediator.
"I'm glad Clinton didn't intervene, because if he did we wouldn't have reached our own agreement," commented package loader Rodriques Dennis.
Strikers hoped to begin returning to work within a few days. But many acknowledged it could take longer as customers slowly returned to UPS service.

"It's good to be going back to work. I'd rather be on the job than on strike, because in a strike both sides lose -- the workers lose and the company loses," said Tom Jones, a part-time UPS package sorter who boasted of having been on picket duty every day since the walkout began.
